title: Mercy asked for
hook: the prayer asks for mercy, not reward (Sukhmani 20)

segments.voice: Yesterday, a beggar at the door, and your line was the same. Did you ask someone for help with something small? The beggar asked for the Name. Today we look at the two words that came before the asking. Day five hundred sixteen.

A loyalty card at a coffee shop. Ten stamps, and the eleventh cup is free. It's a tidy little deal: you do this, you get that. A lot of life runs like that card, and a lot of religion is imagined that way too. Pray enough, give enough, behave well enough, and eventually the reward is stamped and due. Sukhmani's twentieth ashtpadi tucks two small words into the beggar's request that tear the card in half. Kar kirpaa. Today: mercy, asked for.
screen: `TEN STAMPS, ONE FREE CUP.` → `DO THIS, GET THAT.` → `KAR KIRPAA.`

segments.voice: Yesterday's stanza, in paraphrase: the beggar begs for a gift; in Your mercy, give me Your Name. Kar kirpaa: do mercy, show kindness. Kirpaa is grace or mercy, a gift given because the giver is kind, not because the receiver has filled a card. And the word for what's asked, daan, is a gift too: alms, charity. Nothing in that sentence is owed. Day five hundred met the same thread in Japji: actions shape a life, but grace, nadar, opens the gate. Today it's in the beggar's own mouth. Deeds matter; Sikhs are expected to work, serve, and live well. But what the beggar asks for isn't bought by them. It's given, the way a gift is given. Why does that matter on an ordinary Tuesday? Because how you think you're treated tends to become how you treat others. If everything is earned, then the people who've hurt you owe you, and the debt can feel permanent. If you've been met with mercy, the ledger loosens. There's a salok of the poet-saint Kabir, recorded in the Guru Granth Sahib, that makes the link plainly. In paraphrase: where there is forgiveness, there is God Himself. Khimaa, forgiveness, is mercy turned outward. The beggar who asks for kirpaa learns, slowly, to give some away.
screen: `KAR KIRPAA: IN YOUR MERCY.` · `DAAN: A GIFT, NOT WAGES.` · `ASKED AS A GIFT, NOT BOUGHT.` · `KHIMAA: MERCY TURNED OUTWARD.` · then, large: `MERCY, NOT REWARD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: forgive someone. Start small. Not the deepest wound; one of the little ones. A friend who canceled, a driver who cut you off, a sibling's careless comment. Sit, breathe slowly, and picture them. Notice the ledger in your chest: they owe me. On each breath out, loosen it a little. You don't have to excuse what happened. You're simply choosing not to keep stamping the card. If you pray, you can say Waheguru as you let go. The bell holds the time.
Mercy asked for. The beggar asks with kar kirpaa, in Your mercy: the Name is given as a gift, not earned as a wage.
Your line: mercy, not reward. Today, when someone falls short, try answering with a little more mercy than they've earned. Day five hundred sixteen.

howItsDone: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib's twentieth ashtpadi ask for the Name with the words kar kirpaa, in Your mercy, and Gurbani links grace received with forgiveness given.

the beggar asks for the Name as payment for devotion

fork.setup: someone who hurt you in a small way says sorry. by today's lesson, what's the move?
options: make them earn it back, stamp by stamp.
offer a little more mercy than they've earned.
fork.reveal: the beggar who is given mercy learns to give it. Kabir's salok puts it plainly: where there is forgiveness, there is God.

original.note: Gurmukhi: kirpaa, mercy or grace; kar kirpaa, do mercy, opens many requests in Gurbani.

trapdoor: what you thought: mercy asked for means begging to be let off.
what it means: the Name is a gift given in mercy, and those who receive mercy learn to give it.
what a scholar hears: the stanza's words are the vocabulary of gift, daan and kirpaa, and Kabir's salok (jahaa khimaa tah aap) places God where forgiveness is.
